(Sūrat al-Jinn)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: People, both in earlier and in recent times, have disagreed about whether the jinn (unseen beings) exist or not. The apparent report from most of the philosophers (falāsifa) is that they deny them. This is because Abū ʿAlī ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) said in his treatise on the definitions of things: "The jinn are an aerial animal that takes on various forms." Then he said: "This is an explanation of the name." His saying "This is an explanation of the name" indicates that this definition explains the meaning of the word, and that this reality has no existence outside the mind. As for the majority of the adherents of the religions and those who affirm the prophets, they have acknowledged the existence of the jinn. A great number of the earlier philosophers and of the practitioners of spiritual matters (rūḥāniyyāt) also acknowledged them, and they call them the lower spirits (al-arwāḥ al-suflIyya). They claimed that the lower spirits respond more quickly but are weaker, whereas the celestial spirits (al-arwāḥ al-falakiyya) respond more slowly but are stronger.

Those who affirm the jinn differ on two views. Some of them claim that they are not bodies, nor do they inhere in bodies, but are substances subsisting by themselves. They said: "It does not follow from this that they must be equal to the essence of God, because their not being bodies or corporeal is a negation, and sharing in negations does not require equality in quiddity (māhiyya)." They said: "Then these essences, after sharing this negation, are kinds that differ in quiddity, just as the quiddities of accidents differ after being equal in their need for a substrate. Some of them are good, some are evil, some are noble and love good things, and some are base and vile and love evils and calamities. No one knows the number of their kinds and categories except God." They said: "Their being existent immaterial beings does not prevent them from knowing matters of report (akhbariyyāt) or from being able to perform actions." They said: "These spirits can hear, see, know reported matters, and perform specific actions. And since we have said that their quiddities differ, it is not unlikely that among their kinds there are those capable of hard and great actions that human power cannot achieve. It is also not unlikely that each kind has a connection with a specific kind of bodies of this world. Just as the demonstrative proofs of medicine have shown that the first thing attached to the rational soul, which is nothing other than the human being, is the spirits, and these are subtle vaporous bodies that are generated from the finest parts of the blood and formed in the left side of the heart, and then through the soul's attachment to these spirits it becomes attached to the organs through which these spirits flow, it is also not unlikely that each one of these jinn has a connection with a part of the air, so that this part of the air becomes the first thing attached to that spirit. Then, through the flowing of that air into another dense body, those spirits acquire a connection with and control over those dense bodies."

Some people mentioned another way regarding the jinn. They said: "These human spirits and rational souls, when they separate from their bodies and increase in power and perfection because of what is disclosed to them in that spiritual world of hidden secrets, then, if it happens that another body arises which resembles the body that belonged to that separated soul, then because of that similarity a certain attachment to this body arises for that separated soul, for kinship is the cause of union. If this state occurs in good souls, that specific being is called an angel (malak) and that assistance is called inspiration (ilhām). If it occurs in evil souls, that specific being is called a devil (shayṭān) and that assistance is called whispering (waswasa)."

The second view regarding the jinn is that they are bodies. Then the proponents of this doctrine differ on two views. Some of them claim that bodies differ in their quiddities, and that what they share is only one attribute: that they all exist in a place (ḥayyiz), a space (makān) and a direction (jiha), and that they are described by length, breadth and depth. All of these are references to attributes, and sharing in attributes does not require sharing in the complete quiddity, since things that differ in complete quiddity may share one necessary property.

They said: "No one may argue for the similarity of bodies by saying: 'Body, insofar as it is body, has one definition and one reality, so it follows that there should be no variation in the quiddity of body insofar as it is body; rather, if variation occurs, it occurs in a concept additional to that.' Also, we can divide body into subtle and dense, upper and lower, and the locus of division is shared among the divisions, so all the divisions share bodyhood, and variation occurs only through these attributes, namely subtlety and density, and being upper or lower." They said: "These two arguments are weak."

As for the first argument: we say, just as body, insofar as it is body, has one definition and one reality, so accident, insofar as it is accident, has one definition and one reality. It would follow from this that all accidents are equal in complete quiddity, and no rational person says this. Rather, the truth according to the philosophers is that accidents have absolutely no common quiddity among themselves in the essential predicates (dhātiyyāt). For if there were a common quiddity among them, that common element would be a genus for them, and if that were so, the nine categories would not be the highest genera, but would be species of one genus. Once this is established, we say: accidents, insofar as they are accidents, have one reality, yet this does not entail that there is any common essential predicate among them at all, let alone that they are equal in complete quiddity. So why should it not be the case with body as well? For just as accidents differ in complete quiddity, yet those different things are equal in an accidental attribute, namely that they inhere in their subjects, likewise it is permissible that the quiddities of bodies differ in their complete quiddities, and yet they are equal in an accidental attribute, namely that they are perceived by the senses, exist in a place and space, and are described by the three dimensions. This possibility has no refutation at all.

As for the second argument, namely their saying that body can be divided into subtle and dense: it is also refuted by accident, for accident can be divided into quality and quantity, yet it does not follow that there is a common element among them of an essential nature, let alone that they are equal in all essential predicates. So why should it not be the case here as well? If it is established that there is no impossibility in bodies differing, and no proof has shown the invalidity of this possibility, then they say: it is not impossible that among some subtle aerial bodies there is one which differs from the rest of the kinds of air in quiddity, and that this quiddity by its very nature requires a specific knowledge and a specific power to perform wondrous actions. On this supposition, belief in the jinn is quite plausible, and their power to take various forms is also quite plausible.

The second view: the view of those who say that bodies are equal in complete quiddity. The proponents of this doctrine are also two groups.

The first group: those who claim that structure (bunya) is not a condition for life. This is the view of al-Ashʿarī and the majority of his followers, and their arguments on this matter are clear and strong. They said: "If structure were a condition for life, then either it would be said that one single life subsists in the totality of the parts, or it would be said that a separate life subsists in each one of the parts. The first is impossible, because it is inconceivable that one accident inheres in many loci at once. The second is also false, because the parts of which the body is composed are equal, and the life subsisting in each of them is equal to the life subsisting in the other part, and the judgment of a thing is the judgment of its like. So if the subsistence of life in this part depended on the subsistence of that life in that part, the same dependence would arise from the other side, and this would entail a circular dependence, which is impossible. And if this dependence does not arise, then it is established that the subsistence of life in this part does not depend on the subsistence of the second life in that second part. And once this dependence is shown to be false, it is established that it is possible for a single part to be described as living, knowing, powerful and willing. And the view that structure is a condition is refuted."

They said: "As for the argument of the Muʿtazila, namely that structure is necessary, it is nothing but induction (istiqrāʾ): we have observed that whenever the structure is corrupted, life ceases, and whenever it is not corrupted, life remains. Therefore life must depend on the presence of structure. But this is weak, for induction does not yield certainty of necessity. What is the proof that the case of what has not been observed is like the case of what has been observed? Moreover, this argument holds only according to the view of one who denies the breaking of customs (kharq al-ʿādāt), but for one who permits them, this does not fit his doctrine. The difference between them, by making some of them a matter of custom and making others a matter of necessity, is pure arbitrariness with no basis." Thus it is established that structure is not a condition of life. Once this is established, it is not unlikely that God creates in the indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard) knowledge of many matters and power to perform hard and severe actions. At this point the claim that the existence of the jinn is possible becomes clear, whether their bodies are subtle or dense, and whether their parts are large or small.

The second view: that structure is a condition of life, and that there must be firmness in the structure so that it is capable of hard actions. Here there is another issue: is it possible that the object of sight is present, the impediments are removed, the conditions of nearness and distance are fulfilled, and the sense organ is sound, and yet perception still does not occur? Or is this rationally impossible? Al-Ashʿarī and his followers have permitted it, whereas the Muʿtazila have judged it rationally impossible. Al-Ashʿarī argued for his view with rational and transmitted arguments. As for the rational ones, there are two:

The first: We see something large from a distance as small, and this is only because we see some parts of that distant object but not others, although the relation of the sense organ and all the conditions to those visible parts is the same as their relation to the parts that are not visible. So we know that even when the sense organ is sound, the object is present, the conditions are fulfilled and the impediments are absent, perception is not necessarily realized.

The second: A large body has no meaning except as the totality of those composed parts. So when we see that large body at a certain distance, we have seen those parts. Then either the seeing of this part is conditioned on the seeing of that other part

or he would not exist. If the first possibility holds, it entails circularity (dawr), because the parts are alike. If seeing this part depended on seeing that part, then seeing that part would also depend on seeing this part, and circularity would follow. If this dependence does not hold, then seeing a single indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard) at that distance is possible. It is known that such an atom, if it existed alone without any other atoms joined to it, would not be seen. Therefore we know that the occurrence of vision when the conditions are met is not necessary but merely possible.

As for the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), they relied on the argument that if we permitted this, we would also have to permit that drums and trumpets are present before us and we neither see nor hear them. When we counter them with the other ordinary matters and say to them: "Then permit the claim that the waters of the seas have turned into gold and silver, and the mountains into rubies and chrysolite, or that while the eye was closed a thousand suns and moons came into being in the sky, and then when the eye was opened God annihilated them," they are unable to distinguish.

The cause of this confusion is that these Mu'tazilah looked at these regularly recurring matters within the patterns of habit, and they imagined that some of them are necessary and others are not necessary. They did not find a straight rule or a sound basis for distinguishing between the two categories, so the matter became confused for them. Rather, the proper course is to treat all of them alike, and to judge all of them as necessary, as is the view of the philosophers (falasifah), or to judge all of them as not necessary, as is the view of al-Ash'ari (the founder of the Ash'ari school). As for making an arbitrary distinction, that is far-fetched.

When this is established, the possibility of affirming the jinn becomes clear. Even though their bodies are dense and strong, it is still impossible that we should not see them even when they are present. This is according to the view of al-Ash'ari. This is the detailed explanation of these aspects. I am amazed at these Mu'tazilah, how they can believe what has come in the Qur'an about the affirmation of angels and jinn while they persist in their doctrines. This is because the Qur'an indicates that the angels have great power over arduous deeds, and the jinn likewise. This power is not established except in dense and solid bodily organs. Hence it must be that the angel and the jinn are like that. Furthermore, these angels are always present with us: they are the noble scribes and the guardians, and they are also present at the taking of souls. They used to be present with the Messenger (ﷺ), and none of the people saw them. Likewise, the people sitting near one who is in the throes of death do not see anyone. If seeing a dense body is necessary when it is present, then why do we not see them? And if seeing is not necessary, then their doctrine is invalid. If they are described as having power and strength while lacking density and solidity, then their claim that structure is a condition of life is invalid. If they say that they are subtle bodies and living, but that because of their subtlety they cannot perform arduous deeds, this is a denial of the clear statement of the Qur'an. In sum, their position on affirming angels and jinn while holding these doctrines is astonishing. Would that they had mentioned, in support of their doctrines, even a fanciful doubt, let alone a clear proof. This is the warning concerning the subtleties and difficulties in this matter, and success is from God.

The second issue: the reports differ as to whether he (peace be upon him) saw the jinn or not.

The first view, which is the position of Ibn 'Abbas, is that he (peace be upon him) did not see them. He said: "The jinn used to approach the heaven during the interval between Jesus and Muhammad, and they would listen to the news of the heaven and convey it to the soothsayers (kahanah). When God sent Muhammad (peace be upon him), the heaven was guarded and the devils were prevented from the news of the heaven, and meteors were sent against them. They returned to Iblis and informed him of the matter. He said: 'There must be a cause for this. Strike the eastern and western parts of the earth and seek the cause.' A group of those seekers reached Tihamah, and they saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the market of 'Ukaz, praying with his companions the dawn prayer. When they heard the Qur'an they listened to it and said: 'By God, this is the one who came between you and the news of the heaven.' Then they returned to their people and said: 'O our people, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an [﴿سَمِعْنا قُرْآنًا عَجَبًا﴾]' Then God informed Muhammad (peace be upon him) about that unseen matter and said: [﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾] such and such." He said: In this there is evidence that he (peace be upon him) did not see the jinn, for if he had seen them, he would not have attributed the knowledge of this event to revelation, since what is known through direct observation is not attributed in its establishment to revelation.

If it is said: those who were struck by the meteors were the devils, and those who heard the Qur'an were the jinn, so how is the reconciliation? We say: there are two aspects to this:
The first: the jinn were with the devils, and when the devils were struck, the jinn who were with them took up the task of spying for news.
The second: those who were struck by the meteors were from the jinn, but they were called devils, just as the devils of the jinn and of mankind are called such. The devil is every rebel far from obedience to God.

They differed as to who those jinn were who heard the Qur'an. 'Asim related from Abu Dharr, who said: "The delegation of Zawba'ah and his companions came to Mecca to the Prophet (ﷺ), and they heard the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), then they departed." That is the meaning of His saying: [﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn﴾] (al-Ahqaf: 29). It was also said that they were from the Shaysaban, who are the most numerous of the jinn, and most of Iblis's armies are from them.

The second view, which is the position of Ibn Mas'ud, is that he (peace be upon him) was commanded to go to them so that he might recite the Qur'an to them and invite them to Islam. Ibn Mas'ud said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I have been commanded to recite the Qur'an to the jinn. Who will go with me?" They were silent. Then he said it a second time, and they were silent. Then he said it a third time, and 'Abd Allah said: "I said: I will go with you, O Messenger of God." He said: So he set off until, when he came to al-Hajun, near the ravine of Ibn Abi Dubb, he drew a line for me and said: "Do not cross it." Then he went on to al-Hajun, and they descended upon him like locusts, like the men of Zutt, striking their drums as women strike their tambourines, until they enveloped him, and he went out of my sight. I stood up, and he gestured to me with his hand to sit. Then he recited the Qur'an, and his voice continued to rise, and they pressed themselves to the ground until I could hear their voices but could not see them.

In another report: "They said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'What are you?' He said: 'I am the Prophet of God.' They said: 'Who will bear witness to this for you?' He said: 'This tree.' 'Come, O tree!' So it came dragging its roots, with a rattling sound, until it fell before him. He said: 'To what do you bear witness?' It said: 'I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God.' He said: 'Go back.' So it returned as it had come, until it was as it had been." Ibn Mas'ud said: When he came back to me, he said: "Did you want to come to me?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "That was not for you. These jinn came to listen to the Qur'an, then they turned back to their people as warners. They asked me for provisions, so I provided them with bones and dung, so let no one clean himself with a bone or dung."

Know that there is no way to reject the reports. The ways of reconciling the view of Ibn 'Abbas and the view of Ibn Mas'ud are as follows:
One: perhaps what Ibn 'Abbas mentioned happened first, then God revealed this surah to him, and afterwards he was commanded to go out to them, as Ibn Mas'ud related.
Second: even assuming that the event of the jinn happened only once, he (peace be upon him) was commanded to go to them and recite the Qur'an to them, but he (peace be upon him) did not know what they said or what they did, so God revealed to him what they had said and done.
Third: the event happened only once, and he (peace be upon him) saw them and heard their speech, and they believed in him. Then when they returned to their people they said to their people, by way of narration: [﴿Indeed we heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾], and such and such happened. Then God revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) what they had said to their peoples. When these aspects are possible, there is no way to reject the reports.

The third issue: know that His saying, Exalted is He, [﴿Say﴾] (qul), is a command from Him to His Messenger to make known to his companions what God revealed concerning the event of the jinn. In this there are several benefits:
One: that they may know that he (peace be upon him), just as he was sent to mankind, was also sent to the jinn.
Two: that the Quraysh may know that the jinn, despite their rebelliousness, when they heard the Qur'an recognized its inimitability, and so they believed in the Messenger.
Three: that the people may know that the jinn are morally responsible (mukallaf) just like mankind.
Four: that they may know that the jinn listen to our speech and understand our languages.
Five: that it may show that the believer among them calls others of his tribe to faith. In all these aspects there are many benefits, once people come to know them.

The fourth issue: al-wahy (revelation/inspiration) is the casting of a meaning into the soul in a hidden manner, like inspiration (ilham) and the sending down of an angel, and it occurs swiftly, from their saying "al-wahy, al-wahy." The well-known reading is [أُوحِيَ] with an alif. In the transmission of Yunus and Harun from Abu 'Amr it is read [وُحِيَ] with a damma on the waw and without an alif. These are two dialects: it is said wuhiya ilayhi and uhiya ilayhi. It was also read uhiya with a hamzah and without a waw; its origin is wuhiya, and the waw was changed to a hamzah, as one says u'ida and udhina [﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾] (al-Mursalat: 11). His saying, Exalted is He, [﴿that a company of the jinn listened﴾] contains several issues:

The first issue: they all agreed that His saying [﴿annahu istama'a﴾] is with a fatha (on the anna), because it is the substitute for the subject of uhiya, and it is like His saying: [﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾] (al-An'am: 19). They all agreed on the kasra in innā in His saying [﴿Innā sami'nā﴾], because it is a subject (mubtada') quoted after the verb of saying. Here there are two readings:
The first: we carry the rest over the two positions on which we have shown they agreed, so that what is part of the revelation takes a fatha, and what is part of the speech of the jinn takes a kasra. All of them are part of the speech of the jinn except the other two, which are His saying [﴿And that the mosques are for God﴾] (al-Jinn: 18) and [﴿And that when he stood up﴾] (al-Jinn: 19).
The second: the fatha on all of them, and the sense is: [﴿So we believed in it﴾], and that we believed that He, exalted is He, [﴿is the majesty of our Lord﴾], and that [﴿our foolish one used to say about God an outrageous lie﴾], and likewise the rest. If it is said: there is a difficulty here from two aspects:
One: it is improper to attribute belief to some of this surah, for it would be improper to say: "And we believed that he used to say about God an outrageous lie."
Two: one cannot conjoin with a pronoun in the genitive (the hu) except by repeating the governing preposition. One does not say: "We believed in him and Zayd," but rather: "We believed in him and in Zayd." (The answer) to the two difficulties is that if we take His saying "amanna" to mean "we affirmed and testified," both difficulties disappear.

The second issue: a company of the jinn means a group of them, from three to ten. It is reported that this company were Jews. Al-Hasan mentioned that among them were Jews, Christians, Magians, and polytheists. Know further that the jinn related several things.

The first category of what they related is His saying, Exalted is He: [﴿They said: Indeed we heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾] [﴿It guides to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we shall never associate anyone with our Lord﴾]. That is, they said to their people when they returned to them, like His saying: [﴿Then when it was decided, they turned back to their people as warners﴾] (al-Ahqaf: 29). [﴿A wondrous Qur'an﴾] means one that is beyond the limits of its kind and its like. "'Ajaban" is a verbal noun placed in the position of the adjective "'ajib," and there is no doubt that it is more emphatic than "'ajib." [﴿It guides to right conduct﴾] means to what is correct. It was also said: to monotheism (tawhid). [﴿So we believed in it﴾] means in the Qur'an. It is possible that the intended meaning is: "we believed in the right conduct that is in the Qur'an, which is monotheism." [﴿And we shall never associate anyone with our Lord﴾] means: and we shall never return to what we were upon of associating partners with Him. This indicates that those jinn had been among the polytheists.

The second type of what the jinn mentioned is that, just as they disavowed polytheism for themselves, they also declared their Lord free from having a consort or a child. They said: ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, has not taken a consort or a son﴾. On this there are several issues.

The first issue concerns the word *jadd* (majesty). There are two views:

The first: *jadd* in the language means greatness. One says *jadda fulan*, meaning he became great. From this is the hadith: "When a man recited Surat al-Baqarah, he would be *jadda* (honored) among us," meaning his rank was elevated and he became great. A consort is taken out of need for her, and a child for increase through him and for companionship, and these are among the marks of createdness, whereas He, glorified is He, is exempt from every deficiency.

The second view: *jadd* means wealth. From this is the hadith: "The *dhā al-jadd* (the wealthy one) gains nothing from you through his wealth." Abu 'Ubayda said: meaning the wealthy person gains nothing from you through his wealth. Likewise is another hadith: "I stood at the gate of Paradise, and most of those who entered were the poor, while the people of *al-jadd* (wealth) were held back," meaning the wealthy people of the world. Thus the meaning is that He, exalted is He, is free from need of a consort and from finding companionship in a child.

I have a third view on this, which is that the *jadd* of a human being is his origin from which his existence comes. So *jadd* is used metaphorically for origin. His saying, exalted is He: (*jadd* of our Lord) means that the origin of our Lord, that is His specific reality which belongs to that very reality insofar as it is itself necessarily existent, is exalted above all aspects of dependence on another. This is because the one who is necessary in His essence must be necessary in existence in all His aspects, and whatever is like this, it is impossible that He should have a consort or a child.

The second issue: it has been read as *jaddan* (with fatha, as a specifying accusative, *tamyiz*) "rabbuna," and as *jiddu* (with kasra), meaning the truthfulness of His lordship and the rightness of His divinity in being free from taking a consort or a child. It seems that these jinn, when they heard the Qur'an, became aware of the corruption of what the unbelieving jinn held to, so they first turned away from polytheism and second from the religion of the Christians.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: People, both in earlier and in recent times, have disagreed about whether the jinn (unseen beings) exist or not. The apparent report from most of the philosophers (falāsifa) is that they deny them. This is because Abū ʿAlī ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) said in his treatise on the definitions of things: "The jinn are an aerial animal that takes on various forms." Then he said: "This is an explanation of the name." His saying "This is an explanation of the name" indicates that this definition explains the meaning of the word, and that this reality has no existence outside the mind. As for the majority of the adherents of the religions and those who affirm the prophets, they have acknowledged the existence of the jinn. A great number of the earlier philosophers and of the practitioners of spiritual matters (rūḥāniyyāt) also acknowledged them, and they call them the lower spirits (al-arwāḥ al-suflIyya). They claimed that the lower spirits respond more quickly but are weaker, whereas the celestial spirits (al-arwāḥ al-falakiyya) respond more slowly but are stronger.

Those who affirm the jinn differ on two views. Some of them claim that they are not bodies, nor do they inhere in bodies, but are substances subsisting by themselves. They said: "It does not follow from this that they must be equal to the essence of God, because their not being bodies or corporeal is a negation, and sharing in negations does not require equality in quiddity (māhiyya)." They said: "Then these essences, after sharing this negation, are kinds that differ in quiddity, just as the quiddities of accidents differ after being equal in their need for a substrate. Some of them are good, some are evil, some are noble and love good things, and some are base and vile and love evils and calamities. No one knows the number of their kinds and categories except God." They said: "Their being existent immaterial beings does not prevent them from knowing matters of report (akhbariyyāt) or from being able to perform actions." They said: "These spirits can hear, see, know reported matters, and perform specific actions. And since we have said that their quiddities differ, it is not unlikely that among their kinds there are those capable of hard and great actions that human power cannot achieve. It is also not unlikely that each kind has a connection with a specific kind of bodies of this world. Just as the demonstrative proofs of medicine have shown that the first thing attached to the rational soul, which is nothing other than the human being, is the spirits, and these are subtle vaporous bodies that are generated from the finest parts of the blood and formed in the left side of the heart, and then through the soul's attachment to these spirits it becomes attached to the organs through which these spirits flow, it is also not unlikely that each one of these jinn has a connection with a part of the air, so that this part of the air becomes the first thing attached to that spirit. Then, through the flowing of that air into another dense body, those spirits acquire a connection with and control over those dense bodies."

Some people mentioned another way regarding the jinn. They said: "These human spirits and rational souls, when they separate from their bodies and increase in power and perfection because of what is disclosed to them in that spiritual world of hidden secrets, then, if it happens that another body arises which resembles the body that belonged to that separated soul, then because of that similarity a certain attachment to this body arises for that separated soul, for kinship is the cause of union. If this state occurs in good souls, that specific being is called an angel (malak) and that assistance is called inspiration (ilhām). If it occurs in evil souls, that specific being is called a devil (shayṭān) and that assistance is called whispering (waswasa)."

The second view regarding the jinn is that they are bodies. Then the proponents of this doctrine differ on two views. Some of them claim that bodies differ in their quiddities, and that what they share is only one attribute: that they all exist in a place (ḥayyiz), a space (makān) and a direction (jiha), and that they are described by length, breadth and depth. All of these are references to attributes, and sharing in attributes does not require sharing in the complete quiddity, since things that differ in complete quiddity may share one necessary property.

They said: "No one may argue for the similarity of bodies by saying: 'Body, insofar as it is body, has one definition and one reality, so it follows that there should be no variation in the quiddity of body insofar as it is body; rather, if variation occurs, it occurs in a concept additional to that.' Also, we can divide body into subtle and dense, upper and lower, and the locus of division is shared among the divisions, so all the divisions share bodyhood, and variation occurs only through these attributes, namely subtlety and density, and being upper or lower." They said: "These two arguments are weak."

As for the first argument: we say, just as body, insofar as it is body, has one definition and one reality, so accident, insofar as it is accident, has one definition and one reality. It would follow from this that all accidents are equal in complete quiddity, and no rational person says this. Rather, the truth according to the philosophers is that accidents have absolutely no common quiddity among themselves in the essential predicates (dhātiyyāt). For if there were a common quiddity among them, that common element would be a genus for them, and if that were so, the nine categories would not be the highest genera, but would be species of one genus. Once this is established, we say: accidents, insofar as they are accidents, have one reality, yet this does not entail that there is any common essential predicate among them at all, let alone that they are equal in complete quiddity. So why should it not be the case with body as well? For just as accidents differ in complete quiddity, yet those different things are equal in an accidental attribute, namely that they inhere in their subjects, likewise it is permissible that the quiddities of bodies differ in their complete quiddities, and yet they are equal in an accidental attribute, namely that they are perceived by the senses, exist in a place and space, and are described by the three dimensions. This possibility has no refutation at all.

As for the second argument, namely their saying that body can be divided into subtle and dense: it is also refuted by accident, for accident can be divided into quality and quantity, yet it does not follow that there is a common element among them of an essential nature, let alone that they are equal in all essential predicates. So why should it not be the case here as well? If it is established that there is no impossibility in bodies differing, and no proof has shown the invalidity of this possibility, then they say: it is not impossible that among some subtle aerial bodies there is one which differs from the rest of the kinds of air in quiddity, and that this quiddity by its very nature requires a specific knowledge and a specific power to perform wondrous actions. On this supposition, belief in the jinn is quite plausible, and their power to take various forms is also quite plausible.

The second view: the view of those who say that bodies are equal in complete quiddity. The proponents of this doctrine are also two groups.

The first group: those who claim that structure (bunya) is not a condition for life. This is the view of al-Ashʿarī and the majority of his followers, and their arguments on this matter are clear and strong. They said: "If structure were a condition for life, then either it would be said that one single life subsists in the totality of the parts, or it would be said that a separate life subsists in each one of the parts. The first is impossible, because it is inconceivable that one accident inheres in many loci at once. The second is also false, because the parts of which the body is composed are equal, and the life subsisting in each of them is equal to the life subsisting in the other part, and the judgment of a thing is the judgment of its like. So if the subsistence of life in this part depended on the subsistence of that life in that part, the same dependence would arise from the other side, and this would entail a circular dependence, which is impossible. And if this dependence does not arise, then it is established that the subsistence of life in this part does not depend on the subsistence of the second life in that second part. And once this dependence is shown to be false, it is established that it is possible for a single part to be described as living, knowing, powerful and willing. And the view that structure is a condition is refuted."

They said: "As for the argument of the Muʿtazila, namely that structure is necessary, it is nothing but induction (istiqrāʾ): we have observed that whenever the structure is corrupted, life ceases, and whenever it is not corrupted, life remains. Therefore life must depend on the presence of structure. But this is weak, for induction does not yield certainty of necessity. What is the proof that the case of what has not been observed is like the case of what has been observed? Moreover, this argument holds only according to the view of one who denies the breaking of customs (kharq al-ʿādāt), but for one who permits them, this does not fit his doctrine. The difference between them, by making some of them a matter of custom and making others a matter of necessity, is pure arbitrariness with no basis." Thus it is established that structure is not a condition of life. Once this is established, it is not unlikely that God creates in the indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard) knowledge of many matters and power to perform hard and severe actions. At this point the claim that the existence of the jinn is possible becomes clear, whether their bodies are subtle or dense, and whether their parts are large or small.

The second view: that structure is a condition of life, and that there must be firmness in the structure so that it is capable of hard actions. Here there is another issue: is it possible that the object of sight is present, the impediments are removed, the conditions of nearness and distance are fulfilled, and the sense organ is sound, and yet perception still does not occur? Or is this rationally impossible? Al-Ashʿarī and his followers have permitted it, whereas the Muʿtazila have judged it rationally impossible. Al-Ashʿarī argued for his view with rational and transmitted arguments. As for the rational ones, there are two:

The first: We see something large from a distance as small, and this is only because we see some parts of that distant object but not others, although the relation of the sense organ and all the conditions to those visible parts is the same as their relation to the parts that are not visible. So we know that even when the sense organ is sound, the object is present, the conditions are fulfilled and the impediments are absent, perception is not necessarily realized.

The second: A large body has no meaning except as the totality of those composed parts. So when we see that large body at a certain distance, we have seen those parts. Then either the seeing of this part is conditioned on the seeing of that other part

or he would not exist. If the first possibility holds, it entails circularity (dawr), because the parts are alike. If seeing this part depended on seeing that part, then seeing that part would also depend on seeing this part, and circularity would follow. If this dependence does not hold, then seeing a single indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard) at that distance is possible. It is known that such an atom, if it existed alone without any other atoms joined to it, would not be seen. Therefore we know that the occurrence of vision when the conditions are met is not necessary but merely possible.

As for the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), they relied on the argument that if we permitted this, we would also have to permit that drums and trumpets are present before us and we neither see nor hear them. When we counter them with the other ordinary matters and say to them: "Then permit the claim that the waters of the seas have turned into gold and silver, and the mountains into rubies and chrysolite, or that while the eye was closed a thousand suns and moons came into being in the sky, and then when the eye was opened God annihilated them," they are unable to distinguish.

The cause of this confusion is that these Mu'tazilah looked at these regularly recurring matters within the patterns of habit, and they imagined that some of them are necessary and others are not necessary. They did not find a straight rule or a sound basis for distinguishing between the two categories, so the matter became confused for them. Rather, the proper course is to treat all of them alike, and to judge all of them as necessary, as is the view of the philosophers (falasifah), or to judge all of them as not necessary, as is the view of al-Ash'ari (the founder of the Ash'ari school). As for making an arbitrary distinction, that is far-fetched.

When this is established, the possibility of affirming the jinn becomes clear. Even though their bodies are dense and strong, it is still impossible that we should not see them even when they are present. This is according to the view of al-Ash'ari. This is the detailed explanation of these aspects. I am amazed at these Mu'tazilah, how they can believe what has come in the Qur'an about the affirmation of angels and jinn while they persist in their doctrines. This is because the Qur'an indicates that the angels have great power over arduous deeds, and the jinn likewise. This power is not established except in dense and solid bodily organs. Hence it must be that the angel and the jinn are like that. Furthermore, these angels are always present with us: they are the noble scribes and the guardians, and they are also present at the taking of souls. They used to be present with the Messenger (ﷺ), and none of the people saw them. Likewise, the people sitting near one who is in the throes of death do not see anyone. If seeing a dense body is necessary when it is present, then why do we not see them? And if seeing is not necessary, then their doctrine is invalid. If they are described as having power and strength while lacking density and solidity, then their claim that structure is a condition of life is invalid. If they say that they are subtle bodies and living, but that because of their subtlety they cannot perform arduous deeds, this is a denial of the clear statement of the Qur'an. In sum, their position on affirming angels and jinn while holding these doctrines is astonishing. Would that they had mentioned, in support of their doctrines, even a fanciful doubt, let alone a clear proof. This is the warning concerning the subtleties and difficulties in this matter, and success is from God.

* * *

The second issue: the reports differ as to whether he (peace be upon him) saw the jinn or not.

The first view, which is the position of Ibn 'Abbas, is that he (peace be upon him) did not see them. He said: "The jinn used to approach the heaven during the interval between Jesus and Muhammad, and they would listen to the news of the heaven and convey it to the soothsayers (kahanah). When God sent Muhammad (peace be upon him), the heaven was guarded and the devils were prevented from the news of the heaven, and meteors were sent against them. They returned to Iblis and informed him of the matter. He said: 'There must be a cause for this. Strike the eastern and western parts of the earth and seek the cause.' A group of those seekers reached Tihamah, and they saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the market of 'Ukaz, praying with his companions the dawn prayer. When they heard the Qur'an they listened to it and said: 'By God, this is the one who came between you and the news of the heaven.' Then they returned to their people and said: 'O our people, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an [﴿سَمِعْنا قُرْآنًا عَجَبًا﴾]' Then God informed Muhammad (peace be upon him) about that unseen matter and said: [﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾] such and such." He said: In this there is evidence that he (peace be upon him) did not see the jinn, for if he had seen them, he would not have attributed the knowledge of this event to revelation, since what is known through direct observation is not attributed in its establishment to revelation.

If it is said: those who were struck by the meteors were the devils, and those who heard the Qur'an were the jinn, so how is the reconciliation? We say: there are two aspects to this:
The first: the jinn were with the devils, and when the devils were struck, the jinn who were with them took up the task of spying for news.
The second: those who were struck by the meteors were from the jinn, but they were called devils, just as the devils of the jinn and of mankind are called such. The devil is every rebel far from obedience to God.

They differed as to who those jinn were who heard the Qur'an. 'Asim related from Abu Dharr, who said: "The delegation of Zawba'ah and his companions came to Mecca to the Prophet (ﷺ), and they heard the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), then they departed." That is the meaning of His saying: [﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn﴾] (al-Ahqaf: 29). It was also said that they were from the Shaysaban, who are the most numerous of the jinn, and most of Iblis's armies are from them.

The second view, which is the position of Ibn Mas'ud, is that he (peace be upon him) was commanded to go to them so that he might recite the Qur'an to them and invite them to Islam. Ibn Mas'ud said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I have been commanded to recite the Qur'an to the jinn. Who will go with me?" They were silent. Then he said it a second time, and they were silent. Then he said it a third time, and 'Abd Allah said: "I said: I will go with you, O Messenger of God." He said: So he set off until, when he came to al-Hajun, near the ravine of Ibn Abi Dubb, he drew a line for me and said: "Do not cross it." Then he went on to al-Hajun, and they descended upon him like locusts, like the men of Zutt, striking their drums as women strike their tambourines, until they enveloped him, and he went out of my sight. I stood up, and he gestured to me with his hand to sit. Then he recited the Qur'an, and his voice continued to rise, and they pressed themselves to the ground until I could hear their voices but could not see them.

In another report: "They said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'What are you?' He said: 'I am the Prophet of God.' They said: 'Who will bear witness to this for you?' He said: 'This tree.' 'Come, O tree!' So it came dragging its roots, with a rattling sound, until it fell before him. He said: 'To what do you bear witness?' It said: 'I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God.' He said: 'Go back.' So it returned as it had come, until it was as it had been." Ibn Mas'ud said: When he came back to me, he said: "Did you want to come to me?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "That was not for you. These jinn came to listen to the Qur'an, then they turned back to their people as warners. They asked me for provisions, so I provided them with bones and dung, so let no one clean himself with a bone or dung."

Know that there is no way to reject the reports. The ways of reconciling the view of Ibn 'Abbas and the view of Ibn Mas'ud are as follows:
One: perhaps what Ibn 'Abbas mentioned happened first, then God revealed this surah to him, and afterwards he was commanded to go out to them, as Ibn Mas'ud related.
Second: even assuming that the event of the jinn happened only once, he (peace be upon him) was commanded to go to them and recite the Qur'an to them, but he (peace be upon him) did not know what they said or what they did, so God revealed to him what they had said and done.
Third: the event happened only once, and he (peace be upon him) saw them and heard their speech, and they believed in him. Then when they returned to their people they said to their people, by way of narration: [﴿Indeed we heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾], and such and such happened. Then God revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) what they had said to their peoples. When these aspects are possible, there is no way to reject the reports.

[p. 136]

The third issue: know that His saying, Exalted is He, [﴿Say﴾] (qul), is a command from Him to His Messenger to make known to his companions what God revealed concerning the event of the jinn. In this there are several benefits:
One: that they may know that he (peace be upon him), just as he was sent to mankind, was also sent to the jinn.
Two: that the Quraysh may know that the jinn, despite their rebelliousness, when they heard the Qur'an recognized its inimitability, and so they believed in the Messenger.
Three: that the people may know that the jinn are morally responsible (mukallaf) just like mankind.
Four: that they may know that the jinn listen to our speech and understand our languages.
Five: that it may show that the believer among them calls others of his tribe to faith. In all these aspects there are many benefits, once people come to know them.

The fourth issue: al-wahy (revelation/inspiration) is the casting of a meaning into the soul in a hidden manner, like inspiration (ilham) and the sending down of an angel, and it occurs swiftly, from their saying "al-wahy, al-wahy." The well-known reading is [أُوحِيَ] with an alif. In the transmission of Yunus and Harun from Abu 'Amr it is read [وُحِيَ] with a damma on the waw and without an alif. These are two dialects: it is said wuhiya ilayhi and uhiya ilayhi. It was also read uhiya with a hamzah and without a waw; its origin is wuhiya, and the waw was changed to a hamzah, as one says u'ida and udhina [﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾] (al-Mursalat: 11). His saying, Exalted is He, [﴿that a company of the jinn listened﴾] contains several issues:

The first issue: they all agreed that His saying [﴿annahu istama'a﴾] is with a fatha (on the anna), because it is the substitute for the subject of uhiya, and it is like His saying: [﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾] (al-An'am: 19). They all agreed on the kasra in innā in His saying [﴿Innā sami'nā﴾], because it is a subject (mubtada') quoted after the verb of saying. Here there are two readings:
The first: we carry the rest over the two positions on which we have shown they agreed, so that what is part of the revelation takes a fatha, and what is part of the speech of the jinn takes a kasra. All of them are part of the speech of the jinn except the other two, which are His saying [﴿And that the mosques are for God﴾] (al-Jinn: 18) and [﴿And that when he stood up﴾] (al-Jinn: 19).
The second: the fatha on all of them, and the sense is: [﴿So we believed in it﴾], and that we believed that He, exalted is He, [﴿is the majesty of our Lord﴾], and that [﴿our foolish one used to say about God an outrageous lie﴾], and likewise the rest. If it is said: there is a difficulty here from two aspects:
One: it is improper to attribute belief to some of this surah, for it would be improper to say: "And we believed that he used to say about God an outrageous lie."
Two: one cannot conjoin with a pronoun in the genitive (the hu) except by repeating the governing preposition. One does not say: "We believed in him and Zayd," but rather: "We believed in him and in Zayd." (The answer) to the two difficulties is that if we take His saying "amanna" to mean "we affirmed and testified," both difficulties disappear.

The second issue: a company of the jinn means a group of them, from three to ten. It is reported that this company were Jews. Al-Hasan mentioned that among them were Jews, Christians, Magians, and polytheists. Know further that the jinn related several things.

* *

The first category of what they related is His saying, Exalted is He: [﴿They said: Indeed we heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾] [﴿It guides to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we shall never associate anyone with our Lord﴾]. That is, they said to their people when they returned to them, like His saying: [﴿Then when it was decided, they turned back to their people as warners﴾] (al-Ahqaf: 29). [﴿A wondrous Qur'an﴾] means one that is beyond the limits of its kind and its like. "'Ajaban" is a verbal noun placed in the position of the adjective "'ajib," and there is no doubt that it is more emphatic than "'ajib." [﴿It guides to right conduct﴾] means to what is correct. It was also said: to monotheism (tawhid). [﴿So we believed in it﴾] means in the Qur'an. It is possible that the intended meaning is: "we believed in the right conduct that is in the Qur'an, which is monotheism." [﴿And we shall never associate anyone with our Lord﴾] means: and we shall never return to what we were upon of associating partners with Him. This indicates that those jinn had been among the polytheists.

The second type of what the jinn mentioned is that, just as they disavowed polytheism for themselves, they also declared their Lord free from having a consort or a child. They said: ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, has not taken a consort or a son﴾. On this there are several issues.

The first issue concerns the word *jadd* (majesty). There are two views:

The first: *jadd* in the language means greatness. One says *jadda fulan*, meaning he became great. From this is the hadith: "When a man recited Surat al-Baqarah, he would be *jadda* (honored) among us," meaning his rank was elevated and he became great. A consort is taken out of need for her, and a child for increase through him and for companionship, and these are among the marks of createdness, whereas He, glorified is He, is exempt from every deficiency.

The second view: *jadd* means wealth. From this is the hadith: "The *dhā al-jadd* (the wealthy one) gains nothing from you through his wealth." Abu 'Ubayda said: meaning the wealthy person gains nothing from you through his wealth. Likewise is another hadith: "I stood at the gate of Paradise, and most of those who entered were the poor, while the people of *al-jadd* (wealth) were held back," meaning the wealthy people of the world. Thus the meaning is that He, exalted is He, is free from need of a consort and from finding companionship in a child.

I have a third view on this, which is that the *jadd* of a human being is his origin from which his existence comes. So *jadd* is used metaphorically for origin. His saying, exalted is He: (*jadd* of our Lord) means that the origin of our Lord, that is His specific reality which belongs to that very reality insofar as it is itself necessarily existent, is exalted above all aspects of dependence on another. This is because the one who is necessary in His essence must be necessary in existence in all His aspects, and whatever is like this, it is impossible that He should have a consort or a child.

The second issue: it has been read as *jaddan* (with fatha, as a specifying accusative, *tamyiz*) "rabbuna," and as *jiddu* (with kasra), meaning the truthfulness of His lordship and the rightness of His divinity in being free from taking a consort or a child. It seems that these jinn, when they heard the Qur'an, became aware of the corruption of what the unbelieving jinn held to, so they first turned away from polytheism and second from the religion of the Christians.

It has twenty-eight verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened.﴾ On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: People, both in earlier and in recent times, have disagreed about whether the jinn (unseen beings) exist or not. The apparent report from most of the philosophers (falāsifa) is that they deny them. This is because Abū ʿAlī ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) said in his treatise on the definitions of things: "The jinn are an aerial animal that takes on various forms." Then he said: "This is an explanation of the name." His saying "This is an explanation of the name" indicates that this definition explains the meaning of the word, and that this reality has no existence outside the mind. As for the majority of the adherents of the religions and those who affirm the prophets, they have acknowledged the existence of the jinn. A great number of the earlier philosophers and of the practitioners of spiritual matters (rūḥāniyyāt) also acknowledged them, and they call them the lower spirits (al-arwāḥ al-suflIyya). They claimed that the lower spirits respond more quickly but are weaker, whereas the celestial spirits (al-arwāḥ al-falakiyya) respond more slowly but are stronger.

Those who affirm the jinn differ on two views. Some of them claim that they are not bodies, nor do they inhere in bodies, but are substances subsisting by themselves. They said: "It does not follow from this that they must be equal to the essence of God, because their not being bodies or corporeal is a negation, and sharing in negations does not require equality in quiddity (māhiyya)." They said: "Then these essences, after sharing this negation, are kinds that differ in quiddity, just as the quiddities of accidents differ after being equal in their need for a substrate. Some of them are good, some are evil, some are noble and love good things, and some are base and vile and love evils and calamities. No one knows the number of their kinds and categories except God." They said: "Their being existent immaterial beings does not prevent them from knowing matters of report (akhbariyyāt) or from being able to perform actions." They said: "These spirits can hear, see, know reported matters, and perform specific actions. And since we have said that their quiddities differ, it is not unlikely that among their kinds there are those capable of hard and great actions that human power cannot achieve. It is also not unlikely that each kind has a connection with a specific kind of bodies of this world. Just as the demonstrative proofs of medicine have shown that the first thing attached to the rational soul, which is nothing other than the human being, is the spirits, and these are subtle vaporous bodies that are generated from the finest parts of the blood and formed in the left side of the heart, and then through the soul's attachment to these spirits it becomes attached to the organs through which these spirits flow, it is also not unlikely that each one of these jinn has a connection with a part of the air, so that this part of the air becomes the first thing attached to that spirit. Then, through the flowing of that air into another dense body, those spirits acquire a connection with and control over those dense bodies."

Some people mentioned another way regarding the jinn. They said: "These human spirits and rational souls, when they separate from their bodies and increase in power and perfection because of what is disclosed to them in that spiritual world of hidden secrets, then, if it happens that another body arises which resembles the body that belonged to that separated soul, then because of that similarity a certain attachment to this body arises for that separated soul, for kinship is the cause of union. If this state occurs in good souls, that specific being is called an angel (malak) and that assistance is called inspiration (ilhām). If it occurs in evil souls, that specific being is called a devil (shayṭān) and that assistance is called whispering (waswasa)."

The second view regarding the jinn is that they are bodies. Then the proponents of this doctrine differ on two views. Some of them claim that bodies differ in their quiddities, and that what they share is only one attribute: that they all exist in a place (ḥayyiz), a space (makān) and a direction (jiha), and that they are described by length, breadth and depth. All of these are references to attributes, and sharing in attributes does not require sharing in the complete quiddity, since things that differ in complete quiddity may share one necessary property.

They said: "No one may argue for the similarity of bodies by saying: 'Body, insofar as it is body, has one definition and one reality, so it follows that there should be no variation in the quiddity of body insofar as it is body; rather, if variation occurs, it occurs in a concept additional to that.' Also, we can divide body into subtle and dense, upper and lower, and the locus of division is shared among the divisions, so all the divisions share bodyhood, and variation occurs only through these attributes, namely subtlety and density, and being upper or lower." They said: "These two arguments are weak."

As for the first argument: we say, just as body, insofar as it is body, has one definition and one reality, so accident, insofar as it is accident, has one definition and one reality. It would follow from this that all accidents are equal in complete quiddity, and no rational person says this. Rather, the truth according to the philosophers is that accidents have absolutely no common quiddity among themselves in the essential predicates (dhātiyyāt). For if there were a common quiddity among them, that common element would be a genus for them, and if that were so, the nine categories would not be the highest genera, but would be species of one genus. Once this is established, we say: accidents, insofar as they are accidents, have one reality, yet this does not entail that there is any common essential predicate among them at all, let alone that they are equal in complete quiddity. So why should it not be the case with body as well? For just as accidents differ in complete quiddity, yet those different things are equal in an accidental attribute, namely that they inhere in their subjects, likewise it is permissible that the quiddities of bodies differ in their complete quiddities, and yet they are equal in an accidental attribute, namely that they are perceived by the senses, exist in a place and space, and are described by the three dimensions. This possibility has no refutation at all.

As for the second argument, namely their saying that body can be divided into subtle and dense: it is also refuted by accident, for accident can be divided into quality and quantity, yet it does not follow that there is a common element among them of an essential nature, let alone that they are equal in all essential predicates. So why should it not be the case here as well? If it is established that there is no impossibility in bodies differing, and no proof has shown the invalidity of this possibility, then they say: it is not impossible that among some subtle aerial bodies there is one which differs from the rest of the kinds of air in quiddity, and that this quiddity by its very nature requires a specific knowledge and a specific power to perform wondrous actions. On this supposition, belief in the jinn is quite plausible, and their power to take various forms is also quite plausible.

The second view: the view of those who say that bodies are equal in complete quiddity. The proponents of this doctrine are also two groups.

The first group: those who claim that structure (bunya) is not a condition for life. This is the view of al-Ashʿarī and the majority of his followers, and their arguments on this matter are clear and strong. They said: "If structure were a condition for life, then either it would be said that one single life subsists in the totality of the parts, or it would be said that a separate life subsists in each one of the parts. The first is impossible, because it is inconceivable that one accident inheres in many loci at once. The second is also false, because the parts of which the body is composed are equal, and the life subsisting in each of them is equal to the life subsisting in the other part, and the judgment of a thing is the judgment of its like. So if the subsistence of life in this part depended on the subsistence of that life in that part, the same dependence would arise from the other side, and this would entail a circular dependence, which is impossible. And if this dependence does not arise, then it is established that the subsistence of life in this part does not depend on the subsistence of the second life in that second part. And once this dependence is shown to be false, it is established that it is possible for a single part to be described as living, knowing, powerful and willing. And the view that structure is a condition is refuted."

They said: "As for the argument of the Muʿtazila, namely that structure is necessary, it is nothing but induction (istiqrāʾ): we have observed that whenever the structure is corrupted, life ceases, and whenever it is not corrupted, life remains. Therefore life must depend on the presence of structure. But this is weak, for induction does not yield certainty of necessity. What is the proof that the case of what has not been observed is like the case of what has been observed? Moreover, this argument holds only according to the view of one who denies the breaking of customs (kharq al-ʿādāt), but for one who permits them, this does not fit his doctrine. The difference between them, by making some of them a matter of custom and making others a matter of necessity, is pure arbitrariness with no basis." Thus it is established that structure is not a condition of life. Once this is established, it is not unlikely that God creates in the indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard) knowledge of many matters and power to perform hard and severe actions. At this point the claim that the existence of the jinn is possible becomes clear, whether their bodies are subtle or dense, and whether their parts are large or small.

The second view: that structure is a condition of life, and that there must be firmness in the structure so that it is capable of hard actions. Here there is another issue: is it possible that the object of sight is present, the impediments are removed, the conditions of nearness and distance are fulfilled, and the sense organ is sound, and yet perception still does not occur? Or is this rationally impossible? Al-Ashʿarī and his followers have permitted it, whereas the Muʿtazila have judged it rationally impossible. Al-Ashʿarī argued for his view with rational and transmitted arguments. As for the rational ones, there are two:

The first: We see something large from a distance as small, and this is only because we see some parts of that distant object but not others, although the relation of the sense organ and all the conditions to those visible parts is the same as their relation to the parts that are not visible. So we know that even when the sense organ is sound, the object is present, the conditions are fulfilled and the impediments are absent, perception is not necessarily realized.

The second: A large body has no meaning except as the totality of those composed parts. So when we see that large body at a certain distance, we have seen those parts. Then either the seeing of this part is conditioned on the seeing of that other part

or he would not exist. If the first possibility holds, it entails circularity (dawr), because the parts are alike. If seeing this part depended on seeing that part, then seeing that part would also depend on seeing this part, and circularity would follow. If this dependence does not hold, then seeing a single indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard) at that distance is possible. It is known that such an atom, if it existed alone without any other atoms joined to it, would not be seen. Therefore we know that the occurrence of vision when the conditions are met is not necessary but merely possible.

As for the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), they relied on the argument that if we permitted this, we would also have to permit that drums and trumpets are present before us and we neither see nor hear them. When we counter them with the other ordinary matters and say to them: "Then permit the claim that the waters of the seas have turned into gold and silver, and the mountains into rubies and chrysolite, or that while the eye was closed a thousand suns and moons came into being in the sky, and then when the eye was opened God annihilated them," they are unable to distinguish.

The cause of this confusion is that these Mu'tazilah looked at these regularly recurring matters within the patterns of habit, and they imagined that some of them are necessary and others are not necessary. They did not find a straight rule or a sound basis for distinguishing between the two categories, so the matter became confused for them. Rather, the proper course is to treat all of them alike, and to judge all of them as necessary, as is the view of the philosophers (falasifah), or to judge all of them as not necessary, as is the view of al-Ash'ari (the founder of the Ash'ari school). As for making an arbitrary distinction, that is far-fetched.

When this is established, the possibility of affirming the jinn becomes clear. Even though their bodies are dense and strong, it is still impossible that we should not see them even when they are present. This is according to the view of al-Ash'ari. This is the detailed explanation of these aspects. I am amazed at these Mu'tazilah, how they can believe what has come in the Qur'an about the affirmation of angels and jinn while they persist in their doctrines. This is because the Qur'an indicates that the angels have great power over arduous deeds, and the jinn likewise. This power is not established except in dense and solid bodily organs. Hence it must be that the angel and the jinn are like that. Furthermore, these angels are always present with us: they are the noble scribes and the guardians, and they are also present at the taking of souls. They used to be present with the Messenger (ﷺ), and none of the people saw them. Likewise, the people sitting near one who is in the throes of death do not see anyone. If seeing a dense body is necessary when it is present, then why do we not see them? And if seeing is not necessary, then their doctrine is invalid. If they are described as having power and strength while lacking density and solidity, then their claim that structure is a condition of life is invalid. If they say that they are subtle bodies and living, but that because of their subtlety they cannot perform arduous deeds, this is a denial of the clear statement of the Qur'an. In sum, their position on affirming angels and jinn while holding these doctrines is astonishing. Would that they had mentioned, in support of their doctrines, even a fanciful doubt, let alone a clear proof. This is the warning concerning the subtleties and difficulties in this matter, and success is from God.

The second issue: the reports differ as to whether he (peace be upon him) saw the jinn or not.

The first view, which is the position of Ibn 'Abbas, is that he (peace be upon him) did not see them. He said: "The jinn used to approach the heaven during the interval between Jesus and Muhammad, and they would listen to the news of the heaven and convey it to the soothsayers (kahanah). When God sent Muhammad (peace be upon him), the heaven was guarded and the devils were prevented from the news of the heaven, and meteors were sent against them. They returned to Iblis and informed him of the matter. He said: 'There must be a cause for this. Strike the eastern and western parts of the earth and seek the cause.' A group of those seekers reached Tihamah, and they saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the market of 'Ukaz, praying with his companions the dawn prayer. When they heard the Qur'an they listened to it and said: 'By God, this is the one who came between you and the news of the heaven.' Then they returned to their people and said: 'O our people, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an [﴿سَمِعْنا قُرْآنًا عَجَبًا﴾]' Then God informed Muhammad (peace be upon him) about that unseen matter and said: [﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾] such and such." He said: In this there is evidence that he (peace be upon him) did not see the jinn, for if he had seen them, he would not have attributed the knowledge of this event to revelation, since what is known through direct observation is not attributed in its establishment to revelation.

If it is said: those who were struck by the meteors were the devils, and those who heard the Qur'an were the jinn, so how is the reconciliation? We say: there are two aspects to this:
The first: the jinn were with the devils, and when the devils were struck, the jinn who were with them took up the task of spying for news.
The second: those who were struck by the meteors were from the jinn, but they were called devils, just as the devils of the jinn and of mankind are called such. The devil is every rebel far from obedience to God.

They differed as to who those jinn were who heard the Qur'an. 'Asim related from Abu Dharr, who said: "The delegation of Zawba'ah and his companions came to Mecca to the Prophet (ﷺ), and they heard the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ), then they departed." That is the meaning of His saying: [﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn﴾] (al-Ahqaf: 29). It was also said that they were from the Shaysaban, who are the most numerous of the jinn, and most of Iblis's armies are from them.

The second view, which is the position of Ibn Mas'ud, is that he (peace be upon him) was commanded to go to them so that he might recite the Qur'an to them and invite them to Islam. Ibn Mas'ud said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I have been commanded to recite the Qur'an to the jinn. Who will go with me?" They were silent. Then he said it a second time, and they were silent. Then he said it a third time, and 'Abd Allah said: "I said: I will go with you, O Messenger of God." He said: So he set off until, when he came to al-Hajun, near the ravine of Ibn Abi Dubb, he drew a line for me and said: "Do not cross it." Then he went on to al-Hajun, and they descended upon him like locusts, like the men of Zutt, striking their drums as women strike their tambourines, until they enveloped him, and he went out of my sight. I stood up, and he gestured to me with his hand to sit. Then he recited the Qur'an, and his voice continued to rise, and they pressed themselves to the ground until I could hear their voices but could not see them.

In another report: "They said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'What are you?' He said: 'I am the Prophet of God.' They said: 'Who will bear witness to this for you?' He said: 'This tree.' 'Come, O tree!' So it came dragging its roots, with a rattling sound, until it fell before him. He said: 'To what do you bear witness?' It said: 'I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God.' He said: 'Go back.' So it returned as it had come, until it was as it had been." Ibn Mas'ud said: When he came back to me, he said: "Did you want to come to me?" I said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "That was not for you. These jinn came to listen to the Qur'an, then they turned back to their people as warners. They asked me for provisions, so I provided them with bones and dung, so let no one clean himself with a bone or dung."

Know that there is no way to reject the reports. The ways of reconciling the view of Ibn 'Abbas and the view of Ibn Mas'ud are as follows:
One: perhaps what Ibn 'Abbas mentioned happened first, then God revealed this surah to him, and afterwards he was commanded to go out to them, as Ibn Mas'ud related.
Second: even assuming that the event of the jinn happened only once, he (peace be upon him) was commanded to go to them and recite the Qur'an to them, but he (peace be upon him) did not know what they said or what they did, so God revealed to him what they had said and done.
Third: the event happened only once, and he (peace be upon him) saw them and heard their speech, and they believed in him. Then when they returned to their people they said to their people, by way of narration: [﴿Indeed we heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾], and such and such happened. Then God revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) what they had said to their peoples. When these aspects are possible, there is no way to reject the reports.
