The third issue: know that His saying, Exalted is He, [﴿Say﴾] (qul), is a command from Him to His Messenger to make known to his companions what God revealed concerning the event of the jinn. In this there are several benefits:
One: that they may know that he (peace be upon him), just as he was sent to mankind, was also sent to the jinn.
Two: that the Quraysh may know that the jinn, despite their rebelliousness, when they heard the Qur'an recognized its inimitability, and so they believed in the Messenger.
Three: that the people may know that the jinn are morally responsible (mukallaf) just like mankind.
Four: that they may know that the jinn listen to our speech and understand our languages.
Five: that it may show that the believer among them calls others of his tribe to faith. In all these aspects there are many benefits, once people come to know them.

The fourth issue: al-wahy (revelation/inspiration) is the casting of a meaning into the soul in a hidden manner, like inspiration (ilham) and the sending down of an angel, and it occurs swiftly, from their saying "al-wahy, al-wahy." The well-known reading is [أُوحِيَ] with an alif. In the transmission of Yunus and Harun from Abu 'Amr it is read [وُحِيَ] with a damma on the waw and without an alif. These are two dialects: it is said wuhiya ilayhi and uhiya ilayhi. It was also read uhiya with a hamzah and without a waw; its origin is wuhiya, and the waw was changed to a hamzah, as one says u'ida and udhina [﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾] (al-Mursalat: 11). His saying, Exalted is He, [﴿that a company of the jinn listened﴾] contains several issues:

The first issue: they all agreed that His saying [﴿annahu istama'a﴾] is with a fatha (on the anna), because it is the substitute for the subject of uhiya, and it is like His saying: [﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾] (al-An'am: 19). They all agreed on the kasra in innā in His saying [﴿Innā sami'nā﴾], because it is a subject (mubtada') quoted after the verb of saying. Here there are two readings:
The first: we carry the rest over the two positions on which we have shown they agreed, so that what is part of the revelation takes a fatha, and what is part of the speech of the jinn takes a kasra. All of them are part of the speech of the jinn except the other two, which are His saying [﴿And that the mosques are for God﴾] (al-Jinn: 18) and [﴿And that when he stood up﴾] (al-Jinn: 19).
The second: the fatha on all of them, and the sense is: [﴿So we believed in it﴾], and that we believed that He, exalted is He, [﴿is the majesty of our Lord﴾], and that [﴿our foolish one used to say about God an outrageous lie﴾], and likewise the rest. If it is said: there is a difficulty here from two aspects:
One: it is improper to attribute belief to some of this surah, for it would be improper to say: "And we believed that he used to say about God an outrageous lie."
Two: one cannot conjoin with a pronoun in the genitive (the hu) except by repeating the governing preposition. One does not say: "We believed in him and Zayd," but rather: "We believed in him and in Zayd." (The answer) to the two difficulties is that if we take His saying "amanna" to mean "we affirmed and testified," both difficulties disappear.

The second issue: a company of the jinn means a group of them, from three to ten. It is reported that this company were Jews. Al-Hasan mentioned that among them were Jews, Christians, Magians, and polytheists. Know further that the jinn related several things.

The first category of what they related is His saying, Exalted is He: [﴿They said: Indeed we heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾] [﴿It guides to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we shall never associate anyone with our Lord﴾]. That is, they said to their people when they returned to them, like His saying: [﴿Then when it was decided, they turned back to their people as warners﴾] (al-Ahqaf: 29). [﴿A wondrous Qur'an﴾] means one that is beyond the limits of its kind and its like. "'Ajaban" is a verbal noun placed in the position of the adjective "'ajib," and there is no doubt that it is more emphatic than "'ajib." [﴿It guides to right conduct﴾] means to what is correct. It was also said: to monotheism (tawhid). [﴿So we believed in it﴾] means in the Qur'an. It is possible that the intended meaning is: "we believed in the right conduct that is in the Qur'an, which is monotheism." [﴿And we shall never associate anyone with our Lord﴾] means: and we shall never return to what we were upon of associating partners with Him. This indicates that those jinn had been among the polytheists.

The second type of what the jinn mentioned is that, just as they disavowed polytheism for themselves, they also declared their Lord free from having a consort or a child. They said: ﴿And that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, has not taken a consort or a son﴾. On this there are several issues.

The first issue concerns the word *jadd* (majesty). There are two views:

The first: *jadd* in the language means greatness. One says *jadda fulan*, meaning he became great. From this is the hadith: "When a man recited Surat al-Baqarah, he would be *jadda* (honored) among us," meaning his rank was elevated and he became great. A consort is taken out of need for her, and a child for increase through him and for companionship, and these are among the marks of createdness, whereas He, glorified is He, is exempt from every deficiency.

The second view: *jadd* means wealth. From this is the hadith: "The *dhā al-jadd* (the wealthy one) gains nothing from you through his wealth." Abu 'Ubayda said: meaning the wealthy person gains nothing from you through his wealth. Likewise is another hadith: "I stood at the gate of Paradise, and most of those who entered were the poor, while the people of *al-jadd* (wealth) were held back," meaning the wealthy people of the world. Thus the meaning is that He, exalted is He, is free from need of a consort and from finding companionship in a child.

I have a third view on this, which is that the *jadd* of a human being is his origin from which his existence comes. So *jadd* is used metaphorically for origin. His saying, exalted is He: (*jadd* of our Lord) means that the origin of our Lord, that is His specific reality which belongs to that very reality insofar as it is itself necessarily existent, is exalted above all aspects of dependence on another. This is because the one who is necessary in His essence must be necessary in existence in all His aspects, and whatever is like this, it is impossible that He should have a consort or a child.

The second issue: it has been read as *jaddan* (with fatha, as a specifying accusative, *tamyiz*) "rabbuna," and as *jiddu* (with kasra), meaning the truthfulness of His lordship and the rightness of His divinity in being free from taking a consort or a child. It seems that these jinn, when they heard the Qur'an, became aware of the corruption of what the unbelieving jinn held to, so they first turned away from polytheism and second from the religion of the Christians.

The third type of what the jinn said is His saying: ﴿And that the foolish one among us used to speak against Allah an outrageous lie.﴾ Safah (foolishness) is lightness of intellect, and shatat is exceeding the limit in wrongdoing and other things; from it comes "ashatta fi as-sawm" (he went to an extreme in fasting) when he went far in it. That is, he said a statement which in itself is shatat, because of the extreme of what he exceeded in.

Know that since shatat is exceeding the limit, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates whether the intended excess is on the side of negation or on the side of affirmation, it becomes clear that both are blameworthy. Exceeding the limit in negation leads to ta'til (denial of Allah's attributes), and exceeding the limit in affirmation leads to tashbih (anthropomorphism) and the ascription of partners, companions and offspring to Allah. Both are shatat and blameworthy.

The fourth type: His saying: ﴿And we thought that mankind and the jinn would never speak a lie against Allah.﴾ In it there are two issues:

The first issue: the meaning of the verse is that we accepted the words of others only because we thought that a lie would not be attributed to Allah; but when we heard the Qur'an, we knew that they do indeed lie. This is an acknowledgment from them that they fell into those ignorances only because of taqlid (blind imitation), and that they were freed from those darknesses only by the blessing of istidlal (reasoned inference) and ihtijaj (argumentation).

The second issue: concerning His saying "kadhiban" (a lie), by what is it in the accusative? In it there are several views:

First: it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), the estimate being: "that mankind and the jinn would never speak against Allah a statement that is a lie."

Second: it is in the accusative as a masdar, because lying is a type of speech.

Third: whoever reads "an lan taqula" places kadhiban in the position of taqawwulan (fabricating speech), and does not make it an adjective, because taqawwul is only ever a lie.

**The fifth type: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that there were men among mankind who would seek refuge with men among the jinn﴾. On this there are two views.**

**The first**, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun), is that a man in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance), when he travelled and nightfall found him in a barren stretch of land, would say: "I seek refuge with the lord of this valley, or with the mighty one of this place, from the evil of the foolish ones of his people." So he would spend the night under their protection until morning. Others said: when the people of the Jahiliyyah suffered drought, they would send out their scout (ra'id). When he found a place with pasture and water, he would return to his people and call to them. When they reached that land, they would call out: "We seek refuge with the lord of this valley from any calamity befalling us," meaning the jinn. If no one frightened them, they would settle, but sometimes the jinn would frighten them and they would flee.

**The second view** is that the meaning is that there were men among mankind who sought refuge with other men, likewise, but from the evil of the jinn. Such as a man saying: "I seek refuge with the Messenger of Allah from the evil of the jinn of this valley." The proponents of this interpretation only went this way because the word "rajul" (man) refers to a human and not to a jinn. However, this is weak, for no proof has been established that a male jinn is not called "rajul."

As for His saying: ﴿But they increased them in rahaq﴾, the exegetes said: its meaning is that they increased them in sin, audacity, transgression, error, deviation and evil. All of these are from their (the jinn's) own expressions. Al-Wahidi said: "ar-rahaq" (the word *rahaq*) is the covering or overtaking of a thing. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor will darkness cover their faces﴾ [Yunus: 26], and His saying: ﴿Darkness will cover them﴾ [Abasa: 41]. And a man who is *murhaq* means one who is overtaken by those who ask of him.

It is also said: "rahiqatna ash-shams" (the sun overtook us) when it drew near. The meaning is that the men of mankind only sought refuge with the jinn out of fear that the jinn would overtake them. Then they increased in that overtaking: when they sought refuge with them and did not seek refuge with Allah, the jinn made them servile, grew bold against them, and so increased them in oppression. This is the meaning of the saying of 'Ata': "they beat them and choked them."

According to this view, the increase is from the action of the jinn. There is another view regarding the verse, that the increase is from the action of mankind: when mankind sought refuge with the jinn, the jinn increased in transgression because of that seeking of refuge, and so they said: "We have become lords over both jinn and mankind." However, the first view is the one most suited to the context (masaq) of the verse and most in harmony with its arrangement (nazm).

If they are from the speech of the jinn, which is what some of them said to one another, the implied meaning is: "And that mankind thought, as you thought, O jinn." And if they are from the revelation, the implied meaning is: "And that the jinn thought, as you thought, O disbelievers of Quraysh." On either reading, the verse indicates that among the jinn, just as there were polytheists, Jews and Christians, there are those who deny the resurrection. It is also possible that the meaning is that Allah does not send anyone as a messenger, according to the doctrine of the Barahima (Brahmins). Know that interpreting it as the speech of the jinn is preferable, because what precedes it and what follows it is the speech of the jinn, so inserting a statement foreign to the speech of the jinn in between is not fitting.

**Tenth type: His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those beneath that; we were divided into various ways.﴾**

That is, among us are the righteous who fear God, and among us are people beneath that level. The described noun is omitted, as in His words: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164]. Then, who are meant by those who are beneath the righteous? There are two opinions:

The first: they are the *muqtasidun* (those of moderate piety, who are not fully perfect in righteousness).

The second: the intended meaning is anyone who is not complete in righteousness, which includes the *muqtasidun* and the disbelievers. The word *qidad* (ﷺ) comes from *qadad*, like *qit'ah* from *qata'a*. The "ways" (*tara'iq*) are described as *qidad* because the word indicates separation and dispersion. There are several interpretations of the verse:

First: the meaning is "we were people of divergent ways," that is, people of different schools of thought. Al-Suddi said: "The jinn are like you: among them are Murji'ah (*Murji'ah*, a sect that deferred judgment on the sinner's fate), Qadariyyah (*Qadariyyah*, a sect that emphasized human free will), Rafidah (*Rafidah*, a Shi'i group that rejected the early caliphs), and Khawarij (*Khawarij*, the seceding sect that declared grave sinners to be disbelievers)."

Second: we were, in the variation of our conditions, like divergent paths.

Third: our ways were *tara'iq qidad*, with the omission of the annexed noun, which is *al-tara'iq* (the ways), and the pronoun annexed to it taking its place.

**Eleventh type: His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And we have thought that we would never cause God to fail on earth, nor could we escape Him by flight.﴾**

*Al-zann* (ظَنَّ, "to think/suppose") here has the meaning of certainty (*al-yaqin*). The phrases *fi al-ard* (ﷺ, "on earth") and *haraban* (هَرَبًا, "by flight") have two interpretations:

First: both are circumstantial clauses (*hal*). The meaning is: we would never cause Him to fail while we are on the earth, wherever we are in it, and we would never escape Him by fleeing from it to the sky.

Second: we would never cause Him to fail on the earth if He intends a matter for us, and we would never escape Him by flight if He pursues us.

**Twelfth type: His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And we, when we heard the guidance, believed in it. So whoever believes in his Lord will not fear loss or oppression.﴾**

﴿When we heard the guidance﴾: that is, the Qur'an. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. (*Amanna bihi*, آمَنَّا بِهِ, "we believed in it") [al-Qasas: 53], that is, we believed in the Qur'an. ﴿Then he does not fear﴾ (*fa-la yakhaf*, فَلا يَخافُ): so he is not fearful. In this reading, the sentence is understood as containing a nominal clause (*jumlah min al-mubtada' wa al-khabar*), with the prefix (*fa*) introduced before it so that it becomes the response (*jaza'*) of the conditional particle that precedes it. Were it not for that, one would say *la yakhaf* (لا يَخَفْ, without the *fa* and with the jussive). If one asks: what is the benefit of putting the verb in the nominal form (*raf'*), positing an implied subject (*mubtada'*) before it so that it becomes its predicate (*khabar*), and making the *fa* obligatory, when all of that could be dispensed with by simply saying *la yakhaf*? We say: the benefit is that when he does this, it is as if it were said, "so he does not fear," which indicates the certainty that the believer is saved without doubt, and that he alone is singled out for this, not anyone else, because the statement "so he does not fear" means that others would be fearful. Al-A'mash read *fa-la yakhaf* (فَلا يَخَفْ, with the jussive).

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿loss or oppression﴾: *al-bakhs* (البَخْسُ) is deficiency, and *al-rahaq* (الرَّهَقُ) is wrongdoing. There are two interpretations:

First: he does not fear the requital of loss or oppression, because he has not deprived anyone of his right, nor wronged anyone, so he does not fear the consequence of either.

Second: he does not fear being deprived, but is certain that he will be given the full recompense, and he does not fear that humiliation will overtake him, from His words: ﴿humiliation will cover them﴾ [Yunus: 27].

When he reaches its summit, he is pulled down to its base, and then he is compelled to climb again. This is his constant state forever. A parallel to this verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will overwhelm him with an arduous ascent﴾ [al-Muddathir: 17].

**The thirteenth type: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the unjust (al-qasitun). Whoever submits, those have sought out right guidance.﴾**

*Al-qasit* means the wrongdoer who oppresses, and *al-muqsit* means the just one. We have mentioned the meaning of *qasata* and *aqsata* at the beginning of Surat an-Nisa. So *al-qasitun* are the disbelievers who deviate from the path of truth.

It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that when al-Hajjaj wanted to kill him, he said to him: "What do you say about me?" He replied: "You are an unjust one who is also just." The people said: "How well he has spoken!" They thought he was describing him with justice and equity. Al-Hajjaj said: "O fools! He called me a wrongdoer and a polytheist," and he recited to them His saying: ﴿And as for the unjust (al-qasitun)﴾ and His saying: ﴿Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1].

﴿Tahharraw rashadan﴾ means they aimed for the path of truth. Abu 'Ubayda said: *tahharraw* means *tawakhkhaw* (they sought out, they intended). Al-Mubarrad said: the origin of *taharri* is from their saying *dhalika ahra*, meaning "that is more deserving and closer," and *bil-hari an taf'ala kadha*, meaning "it is incumbent upon you to do such-and-such."

Then the jinn condemned the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And as for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell.﴾ Regarding this there are two questions:

[p. 142]

**The first question:** Why did He mention the punishment of the unjust and not the reward of the Muslims? **The answer:** Rather, He did mention the reward of the believers, which is His saying: ﴿Tahharraw rashadan﴾, meaning they sought out a great rectitude whose true reality none but Allah, may He be exalted, can reach. Something of this kind can only be realised in the reward.

**The second question:** The jinn were created from fire, so how can they be fuel for the fire? **The answer:** Although they were created from fire, they changed from that state and became flesh and blood in this manner. It is said: and here ends the speech of al-Hasan.

﴿And that if they had remained upon the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ ﴿That We might test them therein. And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord, He will make him enter a painful punishment.﴾

This is part of what was revealed to him. The implied sense is: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened﴾ [al-Jinn: 1], ﴿and that if they had remained upon the path﴾. So this is the second category of what was revealed to him. Here there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *An* is a lightened form of the heavy (*anna*), and the meaning is: "It was revealed to me that the matter and the account is that if they had remained, such-and-such would have occurred." Al-Wahidi said: the separation of *law* from the verb by the particle is like the separation by *la* and by *sin* in His saying: ﴿that it will not return to them a word﴾ [Ta-Ha: 89] and ﴿He knows that there will be among you the sick﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20].

**The second issue:** To what does the pronoun in His saying *istaqamu* ("they remained") refer? There are two views. Some said: it refers to the jinn who have been mentioned and described earlier, meaning: "These unjust ones, if they had believed, We would have done such-and-such for them."

Others said: rather, the intended referent is humankind, and they argued for this with two points:

The first: the encouragement to benefit from abundant water is only appropriate to humans, not to the jinn.

The second: this verse was revealed after Allah withheld rain from the people of Makkah for years. At most, what this means is that humankind was not mentioned beforehand, but since that was known, it follows the pattern of His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

Al-Qadi said: the closer view is that all of them are included in it. I say: one may argue in support of al-Qadi's view that since He, may He be exalted, established a ruling linked to a cause, which is uprightness, the ruling must be general by the generality of the cause.

**The third issue:** *Al-ghadaq*, with the *dal* either fatha or kasra, means abundant water. It has been read with both. It is said: *ghadiqat al-'aynu* (the spring became abundant), so it is *ghadiqa*; a *rawda mughdiqa* is a meadow abundant in water; and *matarun maghdud*, *ghaydaq* and *ghaydag* refer to rain abundant in water. Regarding the intended meaning of "abundant water" in this verse there are three views:

First: it is the rain and the downpour.

Second, which is the view of Abu Muslim: it is an indication of Paradise, as in His saying: ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Buruj: 11].

Third: it means benefits and goods, and water is used as a metonym for them, because water is the root of all goods in this world.

**The fourth issue:** If we say the pronoun in *istaqamu* refers to the jinn, then there are two views in the verse:

The first: if the jinn had remained upon the best path, that is, if their father, the jinn, had remained upon the worship of Allah which he had, and had not been arrogant in refusing to prostrate to Adam, and had not disbelieved, and his offspring had followed him in Islam, We would have bestowed favour upon them. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and been mindful of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 65], His saying: ﴿And if they had established the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66], His saying: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out and provide for him﴾ [at-Talaq: 2], and His saying: ﴿So I said: Ask forgiveness of your Lord… and He will increase you in wealth and children﴾ [Nuh: 10–12]. He mentioned water only as a metonym for good living and abundance of benefits, since the fitting thing for the jinn is this drinkable water.

The second: the meaning is: if the jinn who heard the Qur'an had remained upon their way which they followed before listening, and had not moved from it to Islam, We would have expanded their provision. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And had it not been that mankind would be one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 33].

Al-Zajjaj preferred the first view. He said: because He mentioned "the path" defined with the article *al-*, it refers to the well-known and familiar path, which is the path of guidance. Those who go to the second interpretation argue for it by His saying after this verse: ﴿That We might test them therein﴾, so it is like His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 178]. The answer to this may be that whoever believes and then Allah bestows blessing upon him, that blessing is also a trial and a test, until it becomes clear whether he will be occupied with gratitude or not, and whether he will spend it in seeking the pleasure of Allah or in the pleasures of desire and Satan.

As for those who said the pronoun refers to humankind, the two views apply to it in exactly the same way. Here, taking His saying ﴿We would have given them abundant water﴾ in its apparent sense is more preferable, because the benefit of humankind from it is more complete and perfect.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** Our companions argued from His saying *li-naftinahum* ("that We might test them") that He, may He be exalted, misguides His servants. The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) answered that *fitnah* means testing, as one says: "I tested the gold with fire," not the creation of misguidance. The Mu'tazilah also used the *lam* in His saying *li-naftinahum* to argue that He, may He be exalted, acts only for a purpose. Our companions answered that the trial is by consensus not something intended, so this verse shows that the *lam* is not for purpose with respect to Allah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord﴾, that is, from His worship, or from His admonition, or from His revelation. *Yaslukhu* (He will make him enter) has also been read with a *nun*, both fatha and damma, meaning "We will cause him to enter." The original form would be *naslukhu fi 'adhab* ("We will make him enter into a punishment"), like His saying: ﴿What has caused you to enter Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddathir: 42]. Nevertheless, this expression is also correct for two reasons:

The first: the implied sense is *naslukhu fi 'adhab*, then the preposition is omitted and the verb is made to reach its object, like His saying: ﴿And Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155].

The second: the meaning of *naslukhu* is *nudkhiluhu* ("We will cause him to enter"). One says *salakahu* and *aslakahu*, both meaning to cause to enter. *Al-Sa'ad* is the verbal noun of *sa'ida*. One says *sa'ida sa'adan* and *su'udan*. So punishment is described by it, because it "ascends" beyond the endurance of the one being punished, that is, it overwhelms him and overpowers him, so he cannot bear it. From this is the saying of 'Umar: "Nothing has ever weighed upon me (ta'sa'adani) as much as the marriage proposal" (a proposal of marriage). He meant: nothing was hard upon me nor overpowered me.

There is another view about it, which was transmitted from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that *sa'ad* is a mountain in Hell, a smooth rock. The disbeliever is compelled to climb it, then he is dragged from in front of him with chains and struck from behind with iron maces, until he reaches its summit after forty years. When he reaches its summit, he is pulled down to its base, and then he is compelled to climb again. This is his constant state forever. A parallel to this verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will overwhelm him with an arduous ascent﴾ [al-Muddathir: 17].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 72, verse 18:

The third category among what was revealed: God Most High's saying, ﴿And the mosques are for God, so do not invoke anyone alongside God﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: The implied construction is: "Say: It has been revealed to me that the mosques are for God." The school of al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, the grammarian) holds that the implied construction is "and because the mosques are for God, so do not invoke," so that the lam (the preposition "because of") is connected to "so do not invoke," meaning: do not invoke anyone alongside God in the mosques, because they belong to God exclusively. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And this your community is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52], according to the meaning: for this reason, worship Me.

The second issue: The scholars differed about the mosques (masajid) in several respects:

The first view, which is the saying of most scholars, is that they are the places built for prayer and the remembrance of God. This includes churches and synagogues as well as the mosques of the Muslims, because the People of the Book would associate others with God in their prayers in their synagogues and churches, so God commanded the Muslims to sincerity and monotheism.

The second: al-Hasan said: by the mosques He meant all the lands. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The earth has been made a mosque for me." It is as if He Most High said: the whole earth is created for God, so do not prostrate upon it to other than its Creator.

The third: It was also narrated from al-Hasan that he said: the mosques are the prayers. According to this view, masajid is the plural of masjad with a fatha on the jim, and masjad in this view is a verbal noun meaning prostration.

The fourth: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the mosques are the limbs upon which the servant prostrates, and these are seven: the two feet, the two knees, the two hands, and the face. This view is the one preferred by Ibn al-Anbari, who said: because these limbs are those upon which prostration falls, and they are created for God Most High, so a sensible person should not prostrate with them to other than God Most High. According to this view, the meaning of masajid is the places of prostration of the body, whose singular is masjad with a fatha on the jim.

The fifth: 'Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: by the mosques He means Makkah with all the mosques in it, because Makkah is the qibla of the world, and everyone prostrates towards it. Al-Wahidi said: The singular of masajid in all these views is masjad with a fatha on the jim, except according to the view of those who say they are the places built for prayer; for its singular is then with a kasra on the jim, because places and verbal nouns are all of this pattern with a fatha on the ayn, except in a number of listed words, namely: al-masjid, al-mat'li', al-mansik, al-maskin, al-manbit, al-mafriq, al-masqit, al-majzir, al-mahshar, al-mashriq, and al-maghrib. In some of them a fatha has also come, namely al-mansak, al-maskan, al-mafraq, and al-matla', and it is permissible in all of them even if not heard.

The third issue: al-Hasan said: it is from the Sunnah that when a man enters the mosque he should say: "There is no god but God," because His saying ﴿so do not invoke anyone alongside God﴾ includes within it a command to remember God and to call upon Him.

The fourth type, among what was revealed, is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the servant of God stood up calling upon Him, they almost became around him a dense crowd.﴾ Know that "the servant of God" ('abd Allah) refers, according to all scholars, to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then al-Wahidi said: this is from the speech of the jinn, not among what was revealed, because it is not fitting for the Messenger to narrate about himself using the third-person form. This is not far-fetched, as in His saying: ﴿The day We shall gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾ [Maryam: 85]. Most scholars hold that it is among what was revealed, since if it were the speech of the jinn, it would have been what is not the speech of the jinn. In the disorder of what is the speech of the jinn, it would be defective and far from soundness of composition. The benefit of this disagreement is that whoever considers it part of what was revealed opens the hamzah in "anna" (that), and whoever considers it the speech of the jinn places a kasrah on it. We will explain the verse according to both views. As for the view that it is among what was revealed, the pronoun in His saying "they almost became" (kadu) refers to whom? There are three possibilities:

The first: it refers to the jinn. The meaning of "stood up calling upon Him" is that he stood worshipping Him, meaning he stood for the dawn prayer when the jinn came to him and listened to the recitation. "They almost became around him a dense crowd" means they pressed upon him, piling up in amazement at what they saw of his worship, and at his companions following him standing, bowing and prostrating, and in admiration of what he recited of the Qur'an, because they saw what they had never seen the like of and heard what they had never heard the like of.

The second: when the Messenger of God came worshipping God alone, differing from the polytheists in their worship of idols, the polytheists, in their mutual support against him and their cooperation in enmity towards him, almost pressed upon him.

The third, which is the statement of Qatadah: when the servant of God stood up, the humans and the jinn gathered together and backed one another against him to nullify the truth he brought and to extinguish the light of God. But God refused except to help him and make him prevail over those who opposed him. As for the view that it is the speech of the jinn, the two possibilities also apply to it. As for His saying "libadan" (a dense crowd), it is the plural of libdah, which is what is piled up, one part upon another, and whatever you stick to something tightly you have "labbadtahu," and from it derives the word for these felts (lubud) that are spread out. It is said "libdat al-asad" (the lion's mane) for the hair that matts between its shoulders, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

[Near a lion, armed and ready to pounce, / with a mane whose claws have not been trimmed.]

It has also been read "lubadan" with a damma on the lam, and "al-lubdah" has the same meaning as "al-libdah." It has been read "lubbadan," the plural of "labid," like "sujjad" and "sajid." It has also been read "lubudan" with a damma on the lam and the ba', the plural of "labud," like "subur," the plural of "sabur." If it is said: why was Muhammad named "servant of God" and not described as "Messenger of God" or "Prophet of God"? We say: because if this statement is among what was revealed, it is fitting for the humility of the Messenger that he should describe himself with servanthood. And if it is the speech of the jinn, the meaning is that when the servant of God occupied himself with the worship of God, why did these disbelievers gather and why did they try to prevent him from it, even though that is what accords with the law of reason?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 72, verses 20–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "I only call upon my Lord and I associate none with Him."﴾ The majority of readers recited qāla (in the third person, "He said") in the form of the absent person (al-ghaybah). ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah recited qul (imperative, "Say"), so that it would match what follows it, which is His saying: ﴿Say: "I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance."﴾ ﴿Say: "No one can grant me protection from Allah, nor will I find any refuge other than Him."﴾

Muqātil said: The disbelievers of Makkah said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You have come with a great matter, and you have antagonized all the people, so turn back from this." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: "I only call upon my Lord."﴾ This is evidence for ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah. As for the one who recited qāla, he understood it to mean that when the people said that, the Prophet ﷺ answered them with his saying: ﴿I only call upon my Lord﴾, so Allah related that from him with His saying "qāla" (he said). Or that may be part of the Jinn's account of the Messenger's circumstances to their people.

﴿Say: "I do not possess for you any harm or any right guidance."﴾ Either "right guidance" (rashad) is interpreted as benefit, so that the sense of the sentence is: "I do not possess for you misguidance (ghayy) or right guidance," and this is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "ghayyan wa-la rashadan." The meaning of the sentence is that the one who benefits and the one who harms, and the one who guides and the one who misleads, is Allah, and that no one among the creation has any power over that.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "No one can grant me protection from Allah."﴾ Muqātil said: They said: "Leave what you call to, and we will protect you," so Allah said to him: ﴿Say: "No one can grant me protection from Allah."﴾

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿nor will I find any refuge other than Him﴾, meaning a place of refuge and shelter. Al-Mubarrad said: "Multaḥadan" is like your saying "munʿaraj" (a place of turning). In the language, iltaḥada means "to incline," so the multaḥad is an entrance into the earth, like a winding burrow that goes into the ground.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 72, verse 23:

Allah's words: ﴿Except a message from Allah and His messages﴾. The commentators have mentioned several interpretations of this exception.

The first: it is an exception from his words "I possess not" (for you), meaning: "I possess not for you any harm or any guidance, except a message from Allah." His words ﴿Say: Indeed, no one will protect me from Him﴾ are a parenthetical clause placed in between, to emphasize the negation of his power and to show his incapacity, with the meaning: if Allah intends harm for him, no one can protect him from it. This is the view of al-Farra' (the grammarian).

The second, which is the view of al-Zajjaj: it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for his words "a refuge" (multaḥadan), and the meaning is: "And I will not find, other than Him, any refuge, except a message," that is, nothing saves me except that I convey from Allah what I have been sent with. He says that this exception is discontinuous (munqati'), because when Allah did not say "and you will not find a refuge," but said "you will not find other than Him a refuge," then the message from Allah does not fall under his words ﴿other than Him a refuge﴾, because a message from Allah is not from other than Allah, but is from Allah and by His help and His grant of success.

The third: some of them said: "illa" (except) means "in", so that its meaning is: "If I do not convey a message," like your saying "illa qiyaman fa-qu'udan" (standing, then sitting), and the meaning is: if I do not convey, I will not find a refuge. If it is said: the well-known usage is "ballagha 'anhu" (he conveyed from him), and he (peace be upon him) said: "Convey from me, convey from me," so why does he say here ﴿a message from Allah﴾? We say: "min" here is not an attribute of the conveying; rather it is in the position of "min" in His words ﴿a declaration of disassociation from Allah﴾ (9:1), with the meaning: a message that is from Allah.

As for His words ﴿and His messages﴾: it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "a message", as if he said: "I possess not for you except the conveying and the messages," and the meaning is: "except that I convey from Allah," so I say "Allah said such-and-such," attributing the speech to Him, and that I convey His messages which He sent me with, without addition or deficiency.

His words ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell﴾. Al-Wahidi said: "inna" is with a kasra because what follows the fa' of the apodosis (jaza') is a position of beginning (ibtida'). For this reason Sibawayh interpreted His words ﴿And whoever returns, then Allah will take retribution from him﴾ (5:95), ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then I will grant him enjoyment﴾ (31:24), ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord, then he does not fear﴾ (72:13) as having an implied subject (mubtada' mudmar). The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has also been read ﴿fa-anna lahu nara jahannam﴾ (with fatha), on the estimate of "then his recompense is that for him is the fire of Hell," as in your saying ﴿then that for Allah is its fifth﴾ (8:41), that is, "then its ruling is that for Allah is its fifth."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, taking into account the plural sense of "whoever." In this verse there are two issues.

The first issue: The majority of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds that the grave sinner is in a middle position and is eternally punished) have used this verse to argue that the sinners among the people of prayer (ahl al-salat) are eternal in the Fire, and that this generality includes them just as it includes the disbelievers. They said: this threat is conditional on the condition that there be no repentance and no greater obedience than it. They said: this generality is stronger in indicating this claim than the other generalities, because in the other generalities there is not the word "forever" (abadan), so the opponent takes "khulud" (abiding) to mean a long stay, whereas here the word "abad" has come, so it is an explicit statement that removes the possibility which the opponent mentioned.

(The answer): We have explained in Surat al-Baqarah the ways of responding to the use of these generalities, and we add here some further ways:

The first: restricting a generality to the particular incident for which the generality was revealed is a well-known custom. For when a woman wants to go out of the house for an hour, and the husband says: "If you go out, you are divorced," this statement applies the oath to that specific hour, so that if she goes out on another day she is not divorced. Here, then, He placed the discourse about conveying from Allah, then said: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning Gabriel: ﴿then indeed for him is the fire of Hell﴾, that is: whoever disobeys Allah in conveying His messages and delivering His revelation, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell. And when what we have mentioned is possible, the argument from it falls away.

The second way: this threat must necessarily cover this case, because it would be ugly to mention, after this incident, a ruling that has no connection to it. So this threat becomes a threat for abandoning conveying from Allah. There is no doubt that abandoning conveying from Allah is among the greatest sins, and the punishment that is consequent upon the greatest sin cannot be consequent upon all sins, because sins that differ in minor and major cannot be equal in punishment. When it is established that this punishment is for this sin, and that what is a punishment for this sin cannot be a punishment for the rest of the sins, we know that this ruling is specific to this sin and does not extend to all sins.

The third way: He mentioned the generalities of the threat in the rest of the verses of the Qur'an without being restricted by the qualifier "forever," and mentioned them here with the qualifier "forever." So this restriction must have a cause, and there is no cause except that this sin is among the greatest sins. And when the cause of this restriction is this meaning, we know that this threat is specific to this sin and does not extend to all sins. And when it is established that this threat is specific to the doer of this sin, the verse becomes indicative that the state of the rest of the sinners is different from that; because His words ﴿then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ mean that this state is for him and not for others, like His words ﴿For you is your religion﴾ (109:6), that is, for you and not for others. And when it is established that they have this state and not others, it is required that for the rest of the sinners there is not the fire of Hell in the manner of perpetuity. So it becomes clear that this verse is a proof for us against them.

Against their citing of the verse there is another objection: His words ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ only cover whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger with all kinds of sins, and that is the disbeliever, and we say that the disbeliever remains in the Fire eternally. We said that His words ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ only cover whoever disobeys Allah with all kinds of sins because His words ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah﴾ allow the exception of all kinds of sins from it, like saying: "And whoever disobeys Allah except in disbelief, and except in fornication, and except in drinking wine." And according to the view of those who hold the doctrine of threat (wa'id) the function of an exception is to exclude what, were it not for it, would have been included under the wording. And if that is so, it is necessary that His words ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah﴾ cover the one who commits all sins, and the one who is like that is the disbeliever. So the verse is specific to the disbeliever on this supposition, and the argument from it falls away.

If it is said: that a single person commits all kinds of sins is impossible, because it is impossible that someone be a believer in anthropomorphism (tajsim) and at the same time a believer in denial of divine attributes (ta'til), and if that is impossible, then applying the verse to it is not permissible. We say: restricting a general term by rational proof is permissible. So our statement ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah﴾ indicates that he commits all kinds of sins; it leaves its application in the respect in which its occurrence is rationally impossible, and it remains covering the one who commits all things that can be combined together. And it is known that combining disbelief with other things is possible, so the verse is specific to it.

The second issue: Those who hold that the imperative (al-amr) indicates obligation (lil-wujub) have cited this verse. They said: one who abandons what is commanded is a disobedient, as in His words ﴿Did you disobey my command?﴾ (20:93), ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ (66:6), ﴿And I will not disobey your command﴾ (18:69). And the disobedient deserves punishment, by His words: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 72, verse 24–25:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when they see that which they are promised, then they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.﴾ If it is asked: what is the thing for which what follows "until" (ḥattā) is the endpoint (ghāyah)? We say: there are two opinions.

The first: it is connected to His saying: ﴿they will be against him a multitude﴾. The sense is that they band together against him in enmity, belittle his helpers, and consider his number insignificant, ﴿until, when they see that which they are promised﴾ from the Day of Badr and Allah's manifestation of him over them, or from the Day of Resurrection, then they will know which of them is weaker in helpers and fewer in number.

The second: it is connected to an omitted element indicated by the state of the disbelievers' belittling of him and their considering his number insignificant. As if it were said: these people will continue in what they are upon, until, when it is such-and-such, it will be such-and-such. Know that the parallel of this verse is His saying in Maryam: ﴿until, when they see that which they are promised, either the punishment or the Hour﴾ [Maryam: 75]. Know also that the disbeliever has no helper nor intercessor on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir: 18], ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28], and each one flees from his companion, as He said: ﴿The Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [Abasa: 34] to the end of it, ﴿The Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed﴾ [al-Hajj: 2]. As for the believers, they have honour, dignity and multitude. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24], and the King, the Holy One, sends peace upon them: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]. There it becomes clear whether the strength and the number lie on the side of the believers or on the side of the disbelievers.

﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term.﴾ Muqatil said: When they heard His saying: ﴿until, when they see that which they are promised, then they will know who is weaker in helpers and fewer in number﴾, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: When will this that you threaten us with happen? Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near﴾ to the end of it. The meaning is that its occurrence is certain, but the time of its occurrence is unknown. His saying: ﴿or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term﴾ means: a limit and a distance. This is like His saying: ﴿And I do not know whether it is near or far, what you are promised﴾ [al-Anbiya: 109]. If it is asked: did he not say, "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and so he knew the nearness of the occurrence of the Resurrection? How then does he say here, "I do not know whether it is near or far"? We say: what is meant by the nearness of its occurrence is that what remains of the world is less than what has passed, and this degree of nearness is known. As for the meaning of knowing the precise nearness, and its absence, that is unknown.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has chosen.﴾ The word "min" in His saying "min rasul" (from a messenger) is explanatory (tabyin) for "man irtada" (whom He has chosen). It means that none has access to the unseen except the chosen one who is a messenger. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: In this there is a refutation of miracles (karamat), for those to whom miracles are attributed, even if they are chosen friends of God (awliya' murtadun), are not messengers, and God has specifically singled out the messengers from among the chosen for knowledge of the unseen. In it there is also a refutation of soothsaying (kihanah), magic (sihr) and astrology (tanjim), for their practitioners are the furthest thing from being chosen and the most deserving of divine wrath. Al-Wahidi said: In this there is evidence that whoever claims that the stars indicate to him what will happen of life or death or other than that, has disbelieved in what is in the Qur'an.

Know that al-Wahidi permits miracles, and that God may inspire His friends (awliya') with the occurrence of some events in the future. The relation of the verse to both cases is one: if he takes the verse as indicating the prohibition of astrological judgments, he should take it as indicating the prohibition of miracles, according to what al-Zamakhshari said; and if he claims that it does not indicate the prohibition of inspirations granted to the friends of God, then he should not take it as indicating the prohibition of astral indications. As for arbitrarily asserting that it indicates the prohibition of astrological judgments but does not indicate the inspirations granted to the friends of God, this is mere whim. In my view, the verse contains no indication of any of what they have said. What it does indicate is that His saying ﴿of His unseen﴾ has no form of generality (sigha 'umum), so that acting upon its implication suffices with God not disclosing to His creation any one of His unseen matters. We therefore take it to refer to the time of the occurrence of the Resurrection, so that the meaning of the verse is that He does not disclose this unseen to anyone, and no indication remains in the verse that He does not disclose any of the unseen matters to anyone. What confirms this interpretation is that He mentioned this verse immediately after His saying: ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term﴾, meaning: I do not know the time of the occurrence of the Resurrection. Then He said after it: ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone﴾, i.e., the time of the occurrence of the Resurrection, from the unseen which God does not disclose to anyone. In sum, His saying ﴿His unseen﴾ is a singular noun in the genitive construction, so acting upon it suffices by taking it to refer to one unseen matter. As for generality, there is no indication in the wording of it. If it is said: when you take that to refer to the Resurrection, how then did He say ﴿except to a messenger whom He has chosen﴾, given that He does not disclose this unseen to any of His messengers? We say: rather, He discloses it near the establishment of the Resurrection. And how not, since He said: ﴿And on the day the sky is split open with clouds and the angels are sent down in procession﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. There is no doubt that the angels know at that time that the Resurrection has come. Also, it is possible that this exception is disjunctive (munqati'), as if He said: He is the Knower of the unseen, so He does not disclose to anyone His specific unseen, which is the establishment of the Resurrection; then He said after it: but whoever of the messengers He has chosen, ﴿for indeed He makes a path before him and behind him﴾ guardians who protect him from the evil of the rebellious jinn and men; because He mentioned this statement only in answer to one who asked Him about the time of the occurrence of the Resurrection, by way of mockery of him and belittling of his religion and his claim.

Know that it is necessary to affirm with certainty that God's intent in this verse is not that He does not inform anyone of anything of the unseen matters except the messengers. What indicates this are several considerations:

First: It has been established by reports close to mass-transmission (tawatur) that Shiq and Satih were two soothsayers who foretold the emergence of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) before the time of his emergence, and they were well known among the Arabs for this type of knowledge, to the extent that Kisra returned to them to learn news of our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus it is established that God may inform non-messengers of some of the unseen.

Second: All the people of religions and creeds agree on the validity of the science of interpreting dreams (ilm al-ta'bir), and that the interpreter may inform of the occurrence of future events, and be truthful in it.

Third: The soothsayer of Baghdad whom Sultan Sanjar ibn Malik Shah transported from Baghdad to Khurasan, and whom he asked about future circumstances; she mentioned things, and then they occurred in accordance with her words.

(The author of the book said): May God conclude his life with goodness. I have seen men who are scholars of kalam and philosophy who related about her that she informed of unseen things in detail, and those events came in accordance with her report. Abu al-Barakat exaggerated in his book al-Mu'tabar in describing her condition, and said: I investigated her condition for thirty years until I became certain that she used to inform of unseen matters in an accurate manner.

Fourth: We observe [that] among those with true inspirations, and this is not restricted to the friends of God; rather it may also be found among magicians, someone like this. We see a person whose lot of the unseen is according to the degree of his ascendant, and he is like this in many of his reports, though he may also lie in most of those reports. We see astrological judgments sometimes corresponding and agreeing with matters, though they too lie in many of them. And when this is observed and perceived, the claim that the Qur'an indicates the contrary leads to a disparagement of the Qur'an, and that is false. So we know that the correct interpretation is what we have mentioned. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 72, verse 27:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For He sends before him and behind him guards﴾, the meaning is that He sends (yasluku) from before the one He has approved for the message and from behind him guards (rasadan), i.e., protectors from among the angels who guard him from the whisperings (wasawis) and mixings (takhalit) of the jinn devils until he conveys what has been revealed to him, and from the crowding (zahma) of the human devils so that they do not harm him or injure him. And it is related from al-Dahhak: No prophet was sent except that angels were with him guarding him from the devils who take on the form of an angel.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: He used the singular "messenger" in His saying, ﴿except for whomever He has approved of as a messenger; then indeed He sends before him and behind him﴾, then He used the plural in His saying, ﴿that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾. A parallel to this is what preceded in His saying, ﴿then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein﴾.

The second issue: Whoever holds that God's knowledge is originated (hudūth 'ilm Allah) has argued from this verse, because the meaning of the verse is "that God may know that they have conveyed the message." A parallel to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until We know the strivers﴾ [Muhammad: 31]. (The answer) comes from two aspects:

The first: Qatadah and Muqatil said: "That Muhammad may know that the messengers before him had conveyed the message just as he conveyed the message." On this view, the lam in (liya'lama) is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context, as if it were said: "We informed him of the preservation of the revelation so that he might know that the messengers before him were in the same state as his in conveying the truth." It is also permissible that the meaning is "that the Messenger may know that they have conveyed," i.e., Gabriel and the angels who are sent to the messengers, the messages of their Lord, so he does not doubt them and knows that they are the truth from God.

The second, which is the choice of most of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun): the meaning is "that God may know that the prophets have conveyed the messages of their Lord." Knowledge here is like it in His saying: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142]. The meaning is "that they may convey the messages of their Lord, so that He knows this from them."

The third issue: It was read as liyu'lama (in the passive voice).

﴿And He encompasses what is with them and has counted everything in number.﴾

As for His words ﴿And He encompasses what is with them﴾, they indicate that He, exalted is He, has knowledge of particulars. As for His words ﴿and has counted everything in number﴾, they indicate that He has knowledge of all existing things. If it is said: counting in number occurs only with finite things, while His words "everything" indicate that the number of things is infinite, so a contradiction arises in the verse. We reply: there is no doubt that counting in number occurs only with finite things, but the word "everything" does not indicate that the number of things is infinite. This is because, according to us, "thing" (shay') refers to existing things, and existing things are finite in number. This verse is one of the proofs cited to show that the non-existent is not a thing. For if the non-existent were a thing, the things would be infinite, and His words ﴿and has counted everything in number﴾ would require that those counted things be finite. Then it would follow that they are both finite and infinite, which is impossible. Therefore it must be firmly held that the non-existent is not a thing, so that this contradiction is dispelled.

And God, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. May His blessings and peace be upon the master of the messengers, the seal of the prophets, Muhammad the Prophet, and upon his family and all his companions.
